template.name: exponent_rules
techniques: power of a power: multiply the exponents
quotient of powers: subtract the exponents
work on the coefficient and the variable separately
misconceptions: adding the exponents of a power of a power
multiplying the coefficient by the exponent

concept: Raise every factor to the power, multiplying exponents; then divide, subtracting exponents.

question.prompt: Which expression is equivalent to the expression above for $x \neq 0$?

choices.label: A
choices.why: This takes $(x^4)^3$ as $x^{4 + 3} = x^7$; a power of a power multiplies the exponents: $x^{4 \cdot 3} = x^{12}$.
choices.rationale: Adds the exponents of a power of a power.

choices.label: B
choices.note: the 2 was not raised to the power 3
choices.why: This leaves the coefficient $2$ as it is; every factor inside the parentheses is raised to the power: $2^3 = 8$.
choices.rationale: Raises only the variable, not the coefficient.

choices.label: C
choices.note: 2 times 3 instead of 2 to the power 3
choices.why: This takes $2^3$ as $2 \cdot 3 = 6$; the coefficient is raised to the power: $2^3 = 8$.
choices.rationale: Multiplies the coefficient by the exponent.

steps.title: Multiply the exponents
steps.caption: **Careful:** a power of a power multiplies the exponents: $4 \times 3 = 12$, not $4 + 3 = 7$.

steps.title: Cube each factor
steps.caption: Cube the coefficient: $2^3 = 8$. The exponent of $x$ is $12$.

steps.title: Divide
steps.caption: Divide the coefficients: $8 \div 4 = 2$. Subtract the exponents: $12 - 3 = 9$.

steps.title: Check
steps.caption: A check with $x = 2$ (a check, not a proof).

solution.keyIdea: A power of a power **multiplies** exponents; dividing powers of the same base **subtracts** them.
